findings.mechanism: on_frame() receives a vendor-owned acme_frame per decoded frame and only checksums it and stores its pointer in the replay ring (sink_push -> ring_put). Nothing ever releases/frees the frame, and the project calls no frame-release API; the only vendor calls are acme_codec_open/feed/close. If the decoder hands over ownership of each frame (or pins it until released), native memory grows with every decoded packet.
findings.cause: Frame ownership not returned to the vendor library: the callback has no release call; the ring stores borrowed const pointers it never frees (ring_destroy frees only the slot array).
findings.evidence: Code reading only. libacmecodec and <acme/codec.h> are not installed on this machine (find / found no acme files), so capture cannot be built or run and growth was not measured. tests/test_ring builds and passes but covers only the ring. Check the vendor header for a release/unref function and ownership rules for acme_frame, then confirm with valgrind or ltrace on a build against the real library.

findings.mechanism: Replay ring in sink holds frame pointers.
findings.cause: Fixed capacity of 32 slots, allocated once in ring_create (ring.c:17); ring_put overwrites the oldest slot and never allocates.
findings.evidence: Read ring.c: the container is bounded and the slot array is freed in ring_destroy; test_ring passes. Retaining 32 pointers is constant-size. The pointed-to frames are the suspected leak above, not the ring.
findings.discriminator: ring_put does only a modular index write with count capped at slots, so the ring's own memory is constant regardless of packet count.
